newsitem.title: USA: US needs to improve toxic waste cleanup - watchdog.
newsitem.headline: US needs to improve toxic waste cleanup - watchdog.

text.p: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency needs to do more to control and recoup its costs for cleaning up the nation's worst toxic waste sites, the watchdog arm of Congress said in a report released Friday.
The General Accounting Office said the government had lost $3.8 billion because of delays by EPA in taking steps that were proposed in 1992 to increase its recovery of cleanup costs.
To be sure, the report said the EPA had "made some improvements in its cost recovery program" by getting responsible private parties to fund the majority of cleanups.

"EPA enforcement officials point out, however, that this approach generally leaves the more difficult cleanups for cost recovery action and thus decreases their ability to recover past costs," the report said.

GAO said the agency continued to spend too much on administrative expenses instead of actual cleanup work and had done little to improve audits on billions of dollars worth of Superfund contract charges.
"EPA's regions are still too dependent upon the contractors' own cost proposals to establish the price of cost-reimbursable work," said the report.

"Finally, although EPA has been addressing the weaknesses in contract management, the agency remains vulnerable to overpaying its contractors and not achieving the maximum cleanup work with its limited resources," it said.

The latest assessment came on the heels of another GAO review of Superfund cleanups. It found the average time for identifying the worst toxic waste sites and cleaning them had grown steadily over the last 10 years.

The reviews come at a time when Republicans and Democrats plan to renew debate on bills to overhaul the Superfund cleanup program, including proposals that would shift more costs from polluters to the government.
